_comment: The portfolio roster. Hand-authored, the features.json pattern, gated both directions. EVERY metric is a number measured or read from the project's own surface on its asOf date, OR derived by the gate from this repository; a metric declares one of the two and never both, so there is exactly one owner of its freshness. Never write a number here from memory. Stack tags are drawn from the closed vocabulary below and the gate rejects anything outside it.
_evidenceComment: `url` and `repo` say WHERE A PROJECT LIVES. `evidence` says WHAT DOCUMENTS IT, and the two are separate fields because they answer different questions and rot differently: a product URL changes when the product moves, a citation changes when the writing changes. Three kinds, each verifiable offline. A `post` ref must be a PUBLISHED post in the built corpus and its label must equal that post's title, which is the two-sources-must-agree pattern this file already uses for the chart enums: the label is restated so the gate can argue it, not copied so a reader has to trust it. A `page` ref must be a path routes.ts declares, because a portfolio citing a page this site does not serve is the same silent failure as a search record citing a fragment nothing renders. A `repo` ref must pass the renderer's own URL protocol allowlist. Evidence is OPTIONAL and an entry with none renders none: several of these projects are documented nowhere public, and an empty list is the honest shape for that rather than a reason to invent a citation.
_schemaTypeComment: The schema.org type of the ITEM this card describes, one per entry from a closed set the gate holds closed. It exists because the roster page is not an application: every entry used to be emitted as a SoftwareApplication with an applicationCategory of WebApplication, which was true of the products and false of a page on this site, and a structured-data lie costs a machine reader more than it costs a human one. Two values, SoftwareApplication and WebPage. Adding a third means teaching app/routes/projects.tsx what to emit for it in the same commit, which is what the closed vocabulary makes unavoidable.
_notableComment: `notable` is two or three sentences on what is technically notable, and it is OPTIONAL for the same reason `evidence` is. Where the repository, this site or a published post does not evidence a technical claim, the entry ships WITHOUT the field rather than with a sentence somebody guessed. NO SENTENCE HERE MAY CARRY A BARE NUMBER, hard rule 17, gated by the same scan that reads content/features.json: the metric above is this page's one number channel and it carries its own provenance, so a digit in the prose is a second copy with nowhere to say how old it is.

projects.name: dustinedwards.info
projects.oneLiner: This site, and the reference implementation for everything else here.
projects.description: A personal publishing platform on Cloudflare Workers: server-rendered React Router, posts in D1 with an FTS5 index, media in R2, and a single admin cockpit that commits to git rather than to a database. It demonstrates the discipline the rest of this list is built with, because every claim the site makes about itself is reconciled against the repository by a gate that fails the build when the two disagree.
notable: Markdown in git is the source of truth and D1 holds the only rendered copy, written by two writers, the deploy pipeline and the Worker, through one shared renderer. Every stored row carries the git blob sha of its markdown and a hash of its own render, so a post the editor saved and a post the build produced cannot differ without a stored hash saying so.

The public plane ships no framework script at all. Public routes do not hydrate, so a reader's whole script payload is the prebuilt enhancement bundles the page actually uses, loaded by nonced module tags beside the markup they upgrade, and every page still works with scripting switched off.

There is no second reviewer, so a family of check scripts is the review. Each counting gate carries an executed-count floor measured through its own pipeline, which is what stops the failure mode a pass count hides: a gate that has quietly stopped looking reports exactly what a clean sweep reports.

evidence.label: How this blog stores posts in git and serves them from D1
A blog reading experience that works without JavaScript
Site search on Cloudflare D1 with SQLite full-text search
Designing a color palette the build can check
Every Cloudflare product, and which ones this site runs on
Colophon: the stack, reconciled against the repository

projects.name: Capsid
projects.oneLiner: A namespaced document graph with typed edges, served over MCP.
projects.description: A knowledge store on Workers and D1 that holds versioned markdown canon in per-project namespaces, with typed edges between documents, FTS5 search, an attributed audit log and integrity linting. It demonstrates that an agent's long-term memory can be a governed database with a schema and a review trail rather than a folder of notes, and it is the store this site's own specifications and rulings live in.
notable: Every write returns a hash of what was stored, and passing it back on the next write makes the server refuse an edit whose base has changed, so two sessions colliding on one document end in a rebase instead of a silent overwrite.

A partial edit names the text it replaces and is rejected unless that text appears exactly once in the document, so an anchor that has drifted fails loudly instead of quietly matching the wrong paragraph.
A namespace maps to a fixed set of repositories, and that mapping is the security boundary: anything outside it is refused rather than resolved to the nearest match.

projects.name: Operator MCP wrapper
projects.oneLiner: A thin MCP server over this site's operator API that contains no policy of its own.
projects.description: An MCP server exposing this site's publishing operations to an agent, deliberately built as a transport with no rules in it: every constraint, including the refusal to let an operator perform a post's first publication, is enforced by the site's API and not by the wrapper. It demonstrates the boundary that makes agent-facing tooling safe to expose, which is that the surface an agent talks to should never be the thing deciding what is allowed.
notable: Every constraint lives in the HTTP API underneath, including the one operation an operator may never perform, a post's first publication. The wrapper can therefore be rewritten or replaced without a rule moving with it, and a refusal it returns is the site's refusal rather than its own.

The protocol implementation was chosen by conformance score rather than by preference, and support for the superseded protocol revision is isolated in a single deletable module with a stated retirement condition instead of being spread through the request path.

An agent writes through the same door a human editor writes through, so an agent's change arrives as an ordinary commit and an ordinary row, and the audit trail does not need to know which of the two made it.

evidence.label: Put the rules in the API, not in the MCP server
Building an MCP server on Cloudflare Workers with OAuth
Giving an AI agent write access to a live site

projects.name: Phage discovery roster
projects.oneLiner: The public roster of the phage discovery program's cohorts, served by this site.
projects.description: A year-by-year roster page carrying each cohort's group photograph and the names of its researchers. It is the one page on this site whose content is neither a post nor derived from one, and it exists on the site's own terms rather than a content management system's: the roster is structured data in the repository, edited by commit and rendered by a route.
notable: The roster is structured data in the repository rather than a post body, because a single markdown column would flatten the year-and-names shape the page renders and make every cohort a heading somebody had to keep in order by hand.

Each photograph's real pixel dimensions are recorded per year and rendered as width and height attributes, so the browser reserves the right box before any image arrives and the page does not shift as they load.
It carries names and photographs and no other copy, deliberately. The absence is the page's design rather than an unfinished state, and the alt text was narrowed to match it.

projects.name: Foxhound
projects.oneLiner: Recovery for failed Stripe subscription payments, priced on what it actually recovers.
projects.description: A revenue-recovery layer over Stripe that retries failed recurring charges on a schedule and then escalates to drafted customer sequences when a retry will not fix the underlying decline. It demonstrates a pricing model aligned with the outcome rather than with seats, taking a share only of revenue that was recovered and billing nothing until those funds have been held long enough to be real.
notable: A recovery is attributed before it is billed, and a payment Stripe's own retries would have collected anyway is recorded as baseline and charged nothing, so the fee tracks money the service caused rather than money that arrived while it was running.
Nothing is billed until a recovery has aged past the window in which it could still be refunded, so a merchant is never charged a share of funds that later go back out.

Corporate mail scanners open links with a real browser identity, so a list of known bots cannot see them. The click guard measures the time from send to click instead, and a click faster than a person could act is marked suspect and cannot make a recovery billable.

projects.name: Foxing
projects.oneLiner: A reader and reading-social product built on the public domain.
projects.description: A reading application carrying a curated public-domain library from Standard Ebooks and Project Gutenberg, with progress tracking and social features around what people are reading. It demonstrates that a content product can be assembled from freely licensed sources and still feel deliberate, because the work is in the curation, the typography and the reading state rather than in owning the catalogue.
notable: Cover art is downloaded into the project's own storage rather than linked from wherever it was found, so the catalogue does not rot when an upstream host moves a file or starts refusing hotlinks.

The search index breaks the platform's whole-database export, so backups are taken table by table with the hand-written prose first, and the index's internal tables are deliberately left out because restoring them corrupts the index rather than repairing it.
The hosted catalogue and the books readers merely log share one table, split by where the row came from, and only catalogue rows carry a file the reader can open.

metric.label: public-domain titles offered, per its own catalogue

projects.name: Germomics
projects.oneLiner: A narrative podcast on microbiology and history, on a publishing platform built for it.
projects.description: A narrative podcast on microbiology and its history, distributed through the usual directories, with its own publishing platform behind it. It demonstrates the editorial half of this portfolio rather than the infrastructural one: a subject-matter show that has to earn attention on the storytelling, with the platform staying out of the way.
notable: Publishing is decided when a page is read rather than by a scheduled job, so a post with a future release time stays hidden from every public read until that moment and needs no cron.
The sitemap is built through the same visibility rule the pages use, so a post still waiting for its release time cannot leak to a search engine through discovery.
Listing queries drop the body, the transcript and the audio waveform and hand them back empty so the shared type stays intact, so a page of episode cards never loads a full transcript.
